newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Lawyer to chair HK Jockey Club in handover year.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer to chair HK Jockey Club in handover year.

text.p: A Cambridge-educated lawyer, Wong Chung-hin, has been chosen chairman of Hong Kong's powerful jockey club to lead the former bastion of colonial privilege through the 1997 handover of the British colony to China.
The Hong Kong Jockey Club -- it dropped the appellation "Royal" last June just one year ahead of the transition -- said on Tuesday Wong was elected at the annual general meeting on Monday.
Wong takes over from Sir John Swaine, former chairman of the territory's Legislative Council and a member of one of Hong Kong's most distinguished local families.
Wong, 63, a member of the Jockey Club since 1961, accedes to one of the colony's most important posts, following in the footsteps of Hong Kong's most influential movers and shakers.

Previous chairmen include Larry Yung, chairman of one of the colony's biggest Red Chips -- or China-related conglomerates -- as well as scores of "taipans" as the chiefs of Hong Kong's big trading houses, or hongs, were once known.
The Jockey Club is Hong Kong's oldest institution -- the first horse race was run in 1841 shortly after a naval shore patrol planted the British flag in Hong Kong.
The colony was formally ceded to Britain a year later in the 1842 Treaty of Nanking and the club was founded two years later.
The colonial image has retreated rapidly. In March, the club appointed its first Chinese chief executive, Lawrence Wong, to replace retired British army general Guy Watkins.
As the only legal outlet for a flutter in gambling-mad Hong Kong it generates billions of dollars in taxes and for charity, making it one of the most exclusive institutions.
The club said betting turnover last year rose to HK$80.6 billion (US$11 billion) from HK$73.1 billion in the 1995 season and the club's charitable trust paid out HK$1.09 billion in donations.
